insights.title: The iPaaS Migration Playbook: Moving to Dell Boomi Without Breaking the Business
insights.excerpt: Legacy middleware migrations fail when teams treat them as lift-and-shift exercises. Here's the inventory-first, strangler-pattern approach that keeps the business running while the platform changes underneath it.

sections.heading: Start with an honest inventory
body: Every middleware estate has two interfaces: the ones in the documentation, and the ones actually running. Before any migration planning, build a complete inventory from the running systems — scheduled jobs, file drops, forgotten SFTP endpoints, the flow someone built in 2019 that finance now depends on.

Classify each interface on three axes: business criticality, technical complexity, and change frequency. This classification drives everything else. High-criticality, low-change interfaces are strangler candidates — wrap and proxy them first. Frequently changed flows are rewritten early, while knowledge is fresh.

sections.heading: Strangle, don't big-bang
body: The strangler pattern applies to integration platforms just as it does to applications. Stand up the new Boomi environment alongside the legacy platform and move interfaces one at a time, starting with low-risk flows to build team confidence and operational muscle.
Run parallel where the risk justifies it: critical financial interfaces can execute on both platforms with reconciliation comparing outputs, until confidence is earned and the legacy path is retired.

sections.heading: Design for the new platform, not the old one
body: The most expensive migration mistake is re-creating legacy design decisions on a modern platform. Legacy middleware often forces point-to-point thinking; iPaaS platforms reward canonical models, reusable subprocesses and shared error handling. Take the discount the new platform offers.

That said, modernise deliberately. Rewriting a stable, well-understood interface just to use new features is risk without reward. Change what the move forces you to change; improve what clearly deserves it.

sections.heading: Operational readiness is the real go-live
body: A migration isn't done when interfaces run — it's done when the operations team can run them. Invest in monitoring, alerting, naming standards and runbooks during the build, not after. The goal is an estate your own people understand without calling the migration partner.

insights.title: PI/PO to SAP Integration Suite: Planning the Transition While There's Still Time
insights.excerpt: SAP Process Orchestration's maintenance horizon is fixed. Teams that start planning early get to choose their pace; teams that don't get the pace chosen for them. A practical framing of the move to Integration Suite on BTP.

sections.heading: Why the timeline matters more than the tooling
body: SAP has set the maintenance window for PI/PO, and extended maintenance is a cost decision, not a strategy. The transition to Integration Suite (Cloud Integration, API Management and related capabilities on BTP) is genuinely a different platform — different runtime model, different artefact types, different operations.

The practical implication: treat this as a multi-quarter programme with an early, cheap discovery phase. The expensive surprises in these projects are always discovered late and always involve interfaces nobody documented.

sections.heading: Not every interface should move
body: A transition is a rare opportunity to delete. Interfaces that exist because a project ended years ago, or because a manual process was automated and then un-automated, should be retired rather than migrated. Our rule of thumb: if you can't find an owner for an interface, that's the answer.

For the interfaces that do move, decide per-flow: rebuild natively on Integration Suite, or route via an iPaaS layer like Dell Boomi where the interface is really about connecting SAP to the non-SAP world. Hybrid is normal and legitimate — dogma is the enemy here.

sections.heading: Build the operating model alongside
body: Integration Suite introduces different skills: Cloud Integration flows, API policies, BTP cockpit operations. Plan team enablement as a workstream with budget, not an afterthought. The teams that struggle are the ones whose first day operating the new platform is also their first day using it.

insights.title: Event-Driven EDI: Modernising B2B Document Exchange Without Losing the Plot
insights.excerpt: EDI isn't going anywhere — but the batch-oriented, black-box way most organisations run it should. How event-driven patterns make document flows observable, debuggable and dramatically easier to operate.

sections.heading: The problem with batch thinking
body: Classic EDI runs in batches: files collected, translated, transmitted on schedules. When something fails, the failure surfaces as an absence — a missing invoice, a partner phone call — hours or days after the cause. Batch isn't wrong, but invisibility is.

Event-driven EDI keeps the standards (X12, EDIFACT, AS2 all stay) and changes the nervous system. Every state transition in a document's life — received, translated, acknowledged, delivered, failed — publishes an event.

sections.heading: What the events buy you
body: First, observability: a live view of every document's position, queryable by partner, type or correlation ID. Second, faster failure response: a failed translation publishes an event that routes to a human with context attached, instead of a log entry nobody reads.

Third, and most underrated: analytics become trivial. Partner conformance rates, acknowledgement latency, document volumes by route — all of it falls out of the event stream without bespoke reporting projects.

sections.heading: Start at the edges
body: You don't need to rebuild the translation engine. Wrap your existing EDI platform — whether it's Boomi, a VAN, or something older — so state changes emit events. Build the dashboard, the alerting and the audit trail first. Once the flow is visible, modernising the components underneath it stops being guesswork.
